title: Bayes' Theorem and the Base Rate Fallacy in Medical Testing

paper.title: An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances

hook: A test that is 99% accurate can still be wrong most of the time it comes back positive. Change the prevalence and watch the posterior collapse.

symbols.meaning: sensitivity: probability of a positive test given disease
false positive rate: probability of a positive test given no disease
posterior probability of disease given a positive test

equation.latex: P(D \mid +) = \frac{P(+ \mid D)\,P(D)}{P(+ \mid D)\,P(D) + P(+ \mid \neg D)\,(1 - P(D))}
equation.caption: Posterior probability of disease after a positive test.

explorations.title: Rare disease, accurate test
explorations.predict: If only 1 in 1000 people have the disease and the test is 99% sensitive with a 5% false positive rate, what fraction of positive tests are true positives?
explorations.observe: The posterior is about 0.019. Out of 1000 people, roughly 1 true positive and 50 false positives appear, so most positives are false alarms.
explorations.why: The numerator P(+|D)P(D) = 0.99 × 0.001 = 0.00099 is tiny compared with the denominator, which is dominated by the false-positive term P(+|¬D)(1-P(D)) = 0.05 × 0.999 ≈ 0.04995. The posterior is the ratio of the small numerator to the large denominator.

explorations.title: Common disease, same test
explorations.predict: Now raise prevalence to 0.5 while keeping sensitivity 0.99 and false positive rate 0.05. Does the posterior exceed 0.9?
explorations.observe: The posterior is about 0.952. With half the population diseased, true positives (0.495) vastly outnumber false positives (0.025).
explorations.why: The numerator P(+|D)P(D) = 0.99 × 0.5 = 0.495 now dominates the denominator 0.495 + 0.05 × 0.5 = 0.52, so the posterior is close to 1.

limitation: The model assumes the test result is a single binary outcome and that sensitivity and false positive rate are known exactly and independent of prevalence. In practice these rates are estimated with uncertainty, and prevalence can vary across subgroups, so the posterior is itself uncertain.
misconception: A high test accuracy does not mean a positive result implies a high probability of disease. When the disease is rare, the false positive rate matters more than sensitivity because there are far more healthy people to generate false alarms.

claims.text: The posterior probability of disease given a positive test equals sensitivity times prevalence divided by the total probability of a positive test.
For a rare disease, even a highly sensitive test can yield a low posterior because false positives from the large healthy population dominate the positives.

outcomes.outcome: Compute the posterior probability of disease given a positive test from prevalence, sensitivity and false positive rate.
Interpret the posterior as a count of true positives among all positives out of 1000 people.
Explain why a rare disease produces a low posterior even with an accurate test.
